rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The bee's revelation can mean God inspiring it or placing in its heart knowledge unique to the creature.
rows.anchor: understood by some to refer to God’s inspiring the bee or placing a certain kind of knowledge in its heart that is unique to this creature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awḥā can denote formal scriptural revelation or other divine communication and inspiration, as in several other verses.
rows.anchor: Revealed translates awḥā, which is derived from a root often used in the Quran for Divine Revelation in a formal, scriptural sense

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The bee's revelation may metaphorically describe the instinctive behaviors God implanted in it.
rows.anchor: may simply be a metaphorical way of referring to the innate, instinctual behaviors that God has implanted in the bee

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī allows that bees may possess intelligence, shown by their intricate hexagonal hives and social organization under an obeyed leader.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī suggests that it is at least possible that bees can be said to possess intelligence, including the ability to know God’s commands and prohibitions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A literal reading fits descriptions of creatures as religious communities, praising God, and prostrating to Him.
rows.anchor: all creatures as constituting an ummah, that is, a religious community (6:38)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction concerns bees making hives in mountains, trees, and structures people build.
rows.anchor: construction of hives in the mountains and the trees as well as in that which they build

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: That which people build can refer to human structures and their roofs.
rows.anchor: in the structures and roofs of human buildings (R, Ṭū, Z).

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The phrase may instead refer to beehives people construct to keep bees and obtain honey.
rows.anchor: may also refer to the beehives constructed by human beings for keeping bees and obtaining their honey (Q).

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Following the Lord's easy ways means following the process God taught the bee for making honey.
rows.anchor: follow the process God has taught it for making honey (Z)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Alternatively, the bee is to follow paths to the fruits God ordained it to eat.
rows.anchor: follow the paths by which it may obtain the fruits that God has ordained for it to consume (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The drink of diverse hues from the bees' bellies is honey, which the verse calls healing for people.
rows.anchor: The drink of diverse hues that comes forth from their bellies is honey (Z), wherein there is healing for mankind

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī reads the verse as generally legitimating medical treatment against the view that illness should simply be endured as God's decree.
rows.anchor: this verse legitimates and makes permissable in a general way seeking medicinal treatments for physical ailments

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: When a man reported his brother's stomach ailment, the Prophet prescribed honey; after the first dose failed, he repeated the instruction, said God's truth outlasted the brother's stomach's false report, and the brother recovered.
rows.anchor: The Prophet again instructed the man to feed his brother honey, saying, “God speaks the truth

rows.speaker: Sufi commentators
rows.claim: A knower and seeker who follows God's ways may become, like the bee, a source of spiritual healing for others.
rows.anchor: a knower and seeker of God who follows the ways and commands of the Lord, as does the bee, will, like the bee, become a source of spiritual healing for others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran is also described as a source of healing for humanity.
rows.anchor: The Quran is also described as a source of healing for humanity (10:57; 17:82)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith calls honey a cure for every ailment and the Quran a cure for what is in people's breasts, commending both cures.
rows.anchor: Honey is the cure for every ailment, and the Quran is the cure for that which lies within breasts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both healings come through waḥy, symbolically in the bee's case.
rows.anchor: both of which come about, according to the Quran, through waḥy, or “revelation,” at least symbolically in the case of the bee

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet prohibited killing bees and other animals praised in the Quran, including ants.
rows.anchor: reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet forbade his followers to kill bees and other animals mentioned favorably

rows.speaker: Mālikī school and some al-Shāfiʿī interpretations
rows.claim: These legal interpretations exempt honey from obligatory zakāh.
rows.anchor: According to the Mālikī school of law and some interpretations of al-Shāfiʿī’s view, honey is exempt from the mandatory alms

rows.speaker: some Shiite commentators
rows.claim: Some Shiite readings take the bee as ʿAlī and the Prophet's family, and its diverse drink as Quranic knowledge and wisdom in their teachings that heals spiritually.
rows.anchor: the bee here is a reference to ʿAlīand the family of the Prophet, and the drink of diverse hues refers symbolically to the knowledge of the Quran

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī and al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī and al-Zamakhsharī note this Shiite interpretation but reject its soundness.
rows.anchor: although its soundness is refuted by them

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabrisī traces the interpretation to ʿAlī saying he was the believers' yaʿsūb, a term meaning both male bee and leader or chieftain.
rows.anchor: al-Ṭabrisī indicates that this interpretation derives from ʿAlī’s statement that he was the yaʿsūb of the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ummah may include Abraham's sons Ishmael and Isaac, grandson Jacob, and Jacob's sons.
rows.anchor: the reference to Abraham also includes his sons Ishmael and Isaac, his grandson Jacob, and Jacob’s sons

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Abraham may be a community unto himself because every good quality was combined and perfected in him.
rows.anchor: Abraham constituted a community unto himself insofar as all good qualities were combined and perfected in him

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Another view is that Abraham was the only believer on earth, or at least in his land, at that time.
rows.anchor: because he was the only believer on earth, or at least in his land, at a time when all others there were disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ummah shares a root with imām, a title of spiritual authority given to Abraham and his sons.
rows.anchor: a title of spiritual authority ascribed to Abraham and his sons

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Here ummah can mean a teacher of good or, like an imam, a leader and model for others to follow.
rows.anchor: community is understood by many to mean one who is a teacher of the good

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanīf describes Abraham as a primordial monotheist, neither Jew nor Christian, and is commonly associated with him elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: Ḥanīf denotes a primordial monotheist who is neither a Jew nor a Christian

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic tradition also applies ḥanīf to Muhammad before prophethood and to other pre-Islamic Arabian monotheists.
rows.anchor: used in the Islamic tradition to describe Muhammad’s spiritual life prior to his becoming a prophet and to others who were monotheist even in the Age of Ignorance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanīf refers to one inclined toward Islam's central creed of submission to the One God.
rows.anchor: a person who is inclined toward the central creed of islām, or submission to the One God

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The ḥunafāʾ were said to observe Abrahamic circumcision and pilgrimage rites at the Kaʿbah in Makkah.
rows.anchor: ḥunafāʾ (pl.) were said to observe the Abrahamic rites of circumcision and the ḥajj, or pilgrimage to the Kaʿbah in Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage tells Makkan idolaters Abraham cannot be associated with them because he rejected the idolatry they embraced.
rows.anchor: meant to make it clear to the Makkan idolaters that Abraham cannot be associated with them, nor they with him

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say the Makkans claimed Abraham as their forefather and wrongly believed they followed his creed.
rows.anchor: the Makkans wished to associate themselves with Abraham and wrongly considered themselves to be following the creed of Abraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's choice of Abraham may mean choosing him as a prophet, as an intimate friend, or both.
rows.anchor: God chose Abraham, either as a prophet (R), as He chooses other prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham thanked God unlike the town in the parable, a veiled reference to Makkah, and shared his gratitude with no partner.
rows.anchor: Abraham was thankful for His Blessings, unlike those in the parable of the town (a thinly veiled reference to Makkah) in v. 112

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's blessings included rescue from the fire into which his people threw him, and the sons Isaac and Ishmael.
rows.anchor: being delivered from the fire into which his people had thrown him (21:69; 29:24); his sons, Isaac and Ishmael

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His blessings included being made an imam for mankind and receiving prophethood for himself and his descendants.
rows.anchor: his being made an imām for mankind (2:124; 21:73); the gift of prophethood for himself and his progeny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham also received sound judgment and a sublime reputation praised among religious communities, including pagan Arabs.
rows.anchor: sound judgment (21:51); and his sublime reputation (19:50), meaning that he was and is praised among various religious communities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's good in this world and righteousness in the Hereafter are also mentioned elsewhere.
rows.anchor: That Abraham enjoyed good in this world and will be among the righteous in the Hereafter is also mentioned in 2:130 and 29:27

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage can answer Abraham's prayer for judgment and to be joined with the righteous.
rows.anchor: This verse can be read as a response to Abraham’s prayer in 26:83

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān functions in the Quran as both an adjective for God and one of His proper Names.
rows.anchor: appears in the Quran as an adjective describing God, but also as one of His proper Names

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the Quran's only instance of al-Raḥmān mounting the Throne; other passages also describe God mounting it.
rows.anchor: This verse is the only instance in the Quran where the Compassionate is referred to as mounting the Throne

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name al-Raḥmān has special significance and is closely connected with Allāh; both are Names of the Divine Essence.
rows.anchor: This verse clearly indicates the close connection between the Names Allāh (“God”) and al-Raḥmān (“the Compassionate”), both of which, in traditional Islamic sources, are identified as Names of the Divine Essence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's Most Beautiful Names and their function in Islamic ritual practice are discussed elsewhere.
rows.anchor: For God’s Most Beautiful Names as well as their function in Islamic ritual practice

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī sees Pharaoh's question as an initial stage of a deeper theological inquiry, continued in 26:23.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī notes that the question posed by Pharaoh here was a preliminary stage to his deeper inquiry about God

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators reject a serious theological reading and take Pharaoh's questions as confrontation.
rows.anchor: Other commentators reject the idea that Pharaoh was making a serious theological inquiry into the Nature of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If sincere, Pharaoh's question asks about God's modality, or how He is.
rows.anchor: or how He is who He is.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers by pointing to signs of God's Being, as giver of each thing's creation and guidance; Pharaoh then asks about divine essence.
rows.anchor: When Moses answered Pharaoh by pointing to the signs of God’s Being, citing Him as He Who gives everything its creation, then guides [it]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's essence is beyond all description or definition and inaccessible through human means.
rows.anchor: God’s Essence is above any and all descriptions and definitions and is completely inaccessible through human means

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh asks what became of the earlier generations after death and what God did with them.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh’s question means, “What is the condition of the former generations after death, and what has God done with them?”

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Moses' answer says this is an unfathomable matter known only to God.
rows.anchor: Moses’ reply confirms that knowledge of this matter is an unfathomable affair that none knows but God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book in which this knowledge is recorded is the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: By a Book is meant the Preserved Tablet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage links water with plant life and is compared with other descriptions of creation and rain.
rows.anchor: The relationship between water and vegetal life is discussed in 6:99 and 13:4

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary points to the benefits of cattle discussed in other verses.
rows.anchor: For the benefits of cattle, see 6:142c; 16:5–7c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuhā derives from a root also meaning restraint or prohibition; here it describes rational people who avoid vile acts and thoughts.
rows.anchor: nuhā, which is derived from a root that also connotes “restraining” or “prohibiting”; here it refers to those who, through the use of their rational faculties

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites' rescue and manna and quails parallel other passages; the command to eat good provisions is also treated at 2:57.
rows.anchor: For God’s sending down manna and quails to the Israelites and the command to eat of the good things We have provided you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning against exceeding limits joins excess with ingratitude; 2:61 recounts their request for other foods and the response to their ingratitude.
rows.anchor: Exceed not the limits therein is a warning against excess combined with ungratefulness for the blessings that they had been given

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites later ask Moses for an idol like those worshipped by others and worship an idol while he is on Sinai.
rows.anchor: For the Israelites’ asking Moses to make them an idol similar to the ones they found others worshipping

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed tryst on the Mount's right side refers to receiving the Torah, soon to be given to Moses at Sinai.
rows.anchor: A tryst for the Israelites on the right side of the Mount refers to the reception of the Torah, which would soon be given to Moses at Mt. Sinai

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right side of the Mount is also associated with Horeb, where Moses met God and was chosen as messenger.
rows.anchor: the right side of the Mount in reference to Mt. Horeb, where Moses met God and was chosen as a messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nature and significance of God's forgiveness are discussed in the cited commentary passages.
rows.anchor: For the nature and significance of God’s Forgiveness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses left Aaron over Israel during a forty-day retreat on Sinai, fasting and conversing intimately with God, then hurried to the meeting place.
rows.anchor: Moses appointed Aaron over the Israelites while he spent forty days on Mt. Sinai in retreat, fasting and having intimate discourse with God

rows.speaker: Kl and al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Moses may have hurried to fulfill God's command immediately or from intense desire to speak with Him; he also wanted God to be more content with him.
rows.anchor: It is said that Moses rushed to his meeting place with God in order to fulfill immediately God’s Command (Kl), and out of an intense desire to speak with Him (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's question does not express ignorance; it lets Moses articulate his haste and heightens his awe and reverence.
rows.anchor: God’s question to Moses is not out of ignorance, but rather functions as a means of allowing Moses to articulate to himself the purpose of his haste

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses means that the Israelites have settled at a place near the Mount.
rows.anchor: the Israelites are close upon his footsteps means that they have alighted in a spot close to the Mount

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Sāmirī is explained as a generic title derived from the Israelite tribe al-Sāmirah.
rows.anchor: a generic title derived from the name of the Israelite tribe (al-Sāmirah)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Samaritan is believed to have been a hypocrite who rejected Moses' message inwardly but appeared to accept it.
rows.anchor: The Samaritan is believed to have been a hypocrite who did not accept Moses’ message, but appeared to do so outwardly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' rebuke parallels 7:150; God's good promise is the Torah Israel was to live by.
rows.anchor: God’s goodly Promise refers to His Promise that He would give the Torah to the Israelites to live by

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke recalls the warning that Israel would incur God's wrath through ingratitude.
rows.anchor: where the Israelites are warned of God’s Wrath if they were to be ungrateful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly describes the mountains' destruction on the Last Day.
rows.anchor: The destruction of the mountains on the Last Day is referred to throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: some traditions
rows.claim: The herald is Archangel Seraphiel (Isrāfīl), who some traditions place on Jerusalem's Dome of the Rock on the Last Day or Resurrection to summon people with a powerful voice.
rows.anchor: The reference here is to the Archangel Seraphiel (Isrāfīl), who according to some traditions will be standing on the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem on the Last Day or the Day of Resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seraphiel is also the archangel responsible for the two trumpet blasts.
rows.anchor: Seraphiel is also the archangel responsible for the two blowings of the trumpet

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say Seraphiel calls people after the second blast, making the scene the Day of Resurrection rather than the Last Day.
rows.anchor: Some say that Seraphiel will call people after the second trumpet blast

rows.speaker: IK and al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: The herald has no crookedness because people cannot turn away from him.
rows.anchor: That there will be no crookedness in the herald means that people will not be able to turn away from him

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: People's voices are humbled out of awe.
rows.anchor: Out of awe, peoples’ voices will be humbled

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The murmur is the faint sound of feet as people walk to the Gathering Place; hamsah denotes a camel hoof's pitter-patter.
rows.anchor: The murmur they will hear on this Day is said to be the slight sounds that people’s feet will make

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamsah denotes the pitter-patter sound of a camel's hoofs.
rows.anchor: Murmur translates hamsah, which denotes the pitter-patter sound of a camel’s hoofs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary refers readers to its discussions of intercession on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: For a discussion of intercession on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: some theologians
rows.claim: Some theologians say approval of a person's word includes anyone who testifies to God's Oneness.
rows.anchor: Some theologians say that the reference to with whose word He is content encompasses anyone who testifies to God’s Oneness

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilites
rows.claim: Muʿtazilites restrict this to believers who have not committed major sins.
rows.anchor: Muʿtazilites restrict this status to those who believe and who also have not committed major sins
